catalog_quote: The stress of the voice nearly always rests on the penultimate syllable of a word, as will be seen from what follows. 1. Nouns.— The majority of these are dissyllabic; as, “mî'ma'”=woman, “lê'pô”=foot ... and the accent is always on the first syllable, even though some of them may have a short vowel in the first, and a long vowel in the second syllable, but when their case endings are added, the accent is shifted to the second syllable; as— mî-ma'ma=to a woman. mî-ma'em=a woman (acct. case). audit.recode_to: From 'fixed penult, right edge, weight-blind, recomputed under suffixation' to 'weak stress on the second syllable (left-edge iamb), not shifting under suffixation (Taid 1987: ap'pi:, ap'pi:-ko, ap'pi:-ko-laŋ), with long vowels attracting stress ('i:.sor vs ta.'ke:, Pegu 2010)'; keep Needham 1886 as a dated dialect-specific (Sa:yang) minority report in caution/contra, and drop wcls 'not-applicable'/weight-blind. If the schema cannot express QS-to-length + peninitial, at minimum flag kind as contested and add Taid 1987 / Pegu 2010 to 'contra'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence and the noun/verb accent rules are verbatim on printed pp.3-5 of Needham 1886 in the held page images (leaf n13) and scanned text (lines 468-545); locator correct. Identity is fine: Needham's 'Shaíyâng Miri of Sadiya' is the Sa:yang clan dialect of Mising (listed as a Mising dialect by Taid 1987 p.130 and Pegu 2010 sec. 1.2.5.5). (2) The coding rests entirely on an 1886 colonial outline grammar. Glottolog lists a 1987 LTBA phonology note and a 1991 CIIL grammar; Shodhganga adds 2010 and 2017 phonology-bearing PhDs and a 2025 IITG instrumental rhythm thesis. I fetched sources all open ones. (3) Every modern source that states stress location disagrees with Needham: Taid 1987 p.137 (weak stress, consistently 2nd syllable, examples show no rightward shift under suffixation, so a 4-syllable word is NOT penult-stressed), Pegu 2010 pp.49-51 (disyllables final/iambic

sources.citation: Taid, Tabu. 1987. A short note on Mising phonology. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 10(1): 130-137.
sources.quote: "Word-stress is rather weak in Mising. The stress is realized consistently in the second syllable. Examples are: /a"ppi:/ /a"ppi:ko/ /a"ppi:kolang/ /a"ppi:komi' lo:min/. ... Mising is not a tone language." (stress stays on the 2nd syllable as suffixes are added: ap-PI:-ko-lang, not penult)
sources.note: Native-speaker phonology note; p.137 states weak stress fixed on the 2nd syllable and shows it NOT shifting under suffixation (a"ppi:, a"ppi:ko, a"ppi:kolang) - directly contradicts the Needham-based penult/right-edge coding.

sources.citation: Pagag, Loreina. 2017. Mising phonological processes and repair strategies: a study in Optimality Theory. PhD thesis, The English and Foreign Languages University, Hyderabad. Shodhganga hdl 10603/568446.
sources.quote: "The great majority of the free morphemes in Mising are disyllabic. Such words are stressed on the second syllable." (no further stress/prosody section in the thesis; contents checked)
sources.note: Recent phonology PhD; p.41 independently states disyllables are stressed on the second syllable (third source against Needham's initial-stress disyllables).

sources.citation: Pegu, Jugendra. 2010. Dialectal variations in Mising and the interference of dominant languages. PhD thesis, Tezpur University (xviii+258 pp). Shodhganga hdl 10603/100959.
sources.quote: "Word-stress is not a prominent feature in Mising. The second syllable is often stressed, for instance: asi 'water', imi 'fire', pəbe 'parrot', and mensəruŋ 'fox'. ... In Mising, the final syllable is the more prominent in a disyllabic foot [iambic, right-dominant]. ... Words in which the syllable is heavy, or syllable which ends in a long vowel takes the stress irrespective of its position ... i:sor 'saliva', e:poŋ 'first wife', take: 'crab' ... two rules: (1) syllable quantity insensitive stress rule [final syllable of disyllabic foot] and (2) quantity sensitive stress. ... Tone is not prese
sources.note: Only description with an explicit metrical stress section (pp.49-51): iambic disyllables, long vowels attract stress - contradicts both 'penult' and 'weight-blind' in our record; covers all eight dialects incl. Sa:yang.

sources.citation: Prasad, Bal Ram. 1991. Mising Grammar. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages (x+132 pp). archive.org dli.language.2267.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage PL4001.A21 P7 1991 (also: hathitrust digitized, search-only (in copyright))
sources.quote: Posits three 'suprasegmental phonemes' = rising/falling/level tone; no statement on word-stress placement anywhere in the text layer (grep stress/accent). Its tone claim is explicitly rejected by Taid 1987 and Pegu 2010 ('What Prasad calls to be tone appears to be a vowel [length]').
